draft.title: Conformity
card: Conformity is following the norms and expectations of a group. Norms are the unwritten rules about how members should behave, dress or speak.
People often conform because of social pressure. They may also conform because they want to belong and be accepted.
Conformity can be a free choice and can happen without anyone being told what to do. A person may copy the group simply because they want to fit in.
Conformity can happen in many groups, such as families, schools, workplaces and friendship groups. It does not mean agreeing with every rule, only acting in line with the group.
draft.remember: Conformity is acting in line with a group's norms, often to belong or avoid pressure.

a.q: Which situation is the best example of conformity?
opts: Sam starts wearing the same shoes as his new team
Sam wears a costume to school to protest a rule
Sam starts a new club for people who dislike sport
Sam ignores what his team does and plays his own way
a.why: Sam copies the dress norms of his team to fit in, which is conformity. Wearing a costume to protest a rule goes against a norm, so it is the opposite of conformity.
a.clue: Look for the person who acts in line with the group.

b.q: Priya privately thinks the dress code at her new workplace is silly. She wears the expected clothes anyway, so she fits in with her colleagues. What does this show?
opts: She conforms, even though she disagrees with the norm
She does not conform, because she disagrees with the norm
She conforms only if her manager orders her to
She does not conform, because she was not forced
b.why: Conformity is about acting in line with the group's norms, not about agreeing with them. Priya dresses as expected to belong, so she conforms. Her private view does not change that.
b.clue: Conformity depends on what a person does, not on what they privately think.

a.best: Sam starts wearing the same shoes as his new team

b.best: She conforms, even though she disagrees with the norm

problems.detail: The card defines norms as 'the unwritten rules' only. Norms can also be formal or written, such as laws and official dress codes, which the chapter's sanctions point relies on. Question b also calls a workplace dress code, usually a written rule, a norm, so the card's definition clashes with its own question.
